senses.gloss:
Ketu
(‘that which is known from a distance’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu astronomical works recognise nine प्लनेत्स् and their influence, not only on the human beings, but also on the affairs of the world.
Sūrya (sun), सोम or चन्द्र (moon), मङ्गल or कुज or अङ्गारक (Mars), बुध (Mercury), गुरु or बृहस्पति (Jupiter), शुक्र (Venus) and शनि (Saturn) are the seven प्लनेत्स्, the guardian deities of the seven days of the week. To these seven are added two more प्लनेत्स्: राहु and केतु. They are actually the two ascending and descending nodes of the मोओन्.
As per the accounts in the पुराणस्, राहु, the son of Siṁhikā and कश्यप, was a demon. At the time of distribution of अमृत or nectar to the gods by विष्णु as मोहिनी (the enchantress), he had surreptitiously entered into the line of the gods. As soon as विष्णु discovered it, he cut off राहु’s head by his सुदर्शन discus. Since then the head became known as ‘Rāhu’ and the body as ‘Ketu’.
As per this version केतु is only the body of राहु. He is, therefore, often shown like a serpent’s tail, whereas राहु is depicted only as a head.
In iconographical works केतु has been depicted in several ways:
He is shown as a dark and ugly person, bedecked with ornaments, with two arms, riding on a vulture.
In another account, he is pictured as riding in a chariot dawn by pigeons, holding a गदा (mace) in one hand, with the other showing varadamudrā (bestowal of boons).
As a planet, he is malefic in influence.
Sometimes several forms of केतु (like Dhruvaketu, Chalaketu and Dhūmaketu) are also depicted.
See also RĀHU.
